Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a compact oriented smooth surface and let $j_s$, $0\le s\le1$, be a smooth family of orientation-compatible almost complex structures: $j_s^2=-I$ and $(v,j_sv)$ has positive orientation for every nonzero tangent vector $v$. No integrability hypothesis is imposed.

There is a finite cover of $[0,1]\times\Sigma$ by local maps of the form
$$(s,x)\longmapsto(s,z_s(x))$$
which are smooth diffeomorphisms onto their images and for which every $z_s$ is a complex coordinate for $j_s$. In particular each $j_s$ is integrable and its complex coordinate transitions vary smoothly with the parameter. Near a chosen center a coordinate may be normalized to have value zero and prescribed positive complex-linear derivative obtained by smoothly identifying $j_s$ at that center with $i$.

On a region where the structures and a holomorphic chart are already fixed, those given charts may be included unchanged. This is an actual parametric local coordinate theorem, not an appeal to dimension-two integrability or to a full-choice measurable Riemann mapping theorem.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $j_s$, $s\in[0,1]$, be a smooth family of orientation-compatible almost complex structures on a compact oriented surface $\Sigma$. Fix an integer $m\ge1$. The topological space
$$\mathcal X=([0,1]\times\Sigma^m)/\mathfrak S_m,$$
where permutations act only on the surface factors, has a smooth manifold structure with boundary for which the projection to $[0,1]$ is a proper smooth submersion. Its fiber at $s$ is the complex manifold $\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma,j_s)$, with its usual coefficient coordinates. The fiberwise complex structures are smooth on the vertical tangent bundle. There is a smooth trivialization $\Phi_s:X_0\to X_s$, $\Phi_0=I$, with a genuine smooth permutation-equivariant ordered lift $\widetilde\Phi_s:\Sigma^m\to\Sigma^m$. It satisfies $q_s\widetilde\Phi_s=\Phi_s q_0$, has uniformly bounded derivatives of every fixed order on the compact parameter-product space, preserves every pairwise diagonal and every coordinate incidence hypersurface $\{z_i=p\}$, and is the raw identity wherever $\Phi_s$ is prescribed to be the raw identity.

The trivialization can simultaneously preserve every multiplicity stratum and each of finitely many incidence divisors $E_p=\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}\Sigma$ for prescribed distinct points $p$. It may moreover be chosen to be the identity on a fixed neighborhood, in the underlying unordered-tuple space away from repeated points, of any prescribed compact subset disjoint from those divisors and the repeated-point locus. In particular this applies to a finite union of product tori formed from disjoint attaching circles avoiding those points. On such a torus, if the full endomorphism $j_s$ along every attaching circle is independent of $s$, the pulled-back full vertical complex structure on its ambient tangent bundle is independent of $s$ too. If the family is fixed on a neighborhood of finitely many surface points, the trivialization may also be the identity on coefficient-chart neighborhoods of tuples supported there, whenever these requirements are compatible with the prescribed compact subset.

This constructs smooth maps between the symmetric products using the relative complex family. It makes no assertion that the symmetric power of an arbitrary nonholomorphic surface diffeomorphism is smooth.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,g)$ be compact and let $L_0,L_1\subset X$ be compact smooth submanifolds whose intersections are finite and transverse. Suppose fixed disjoint coordinate neighborhoods of the intersection points take both submanifolds to linear subspaces, as provided by the product generator charts. Then there is a smooth map
$$\mathcal E:\{(x,v)\in TX:|v|_g<\epsilon\}\longrightarrow X$$
for some $\epsilon>0$, with $\mathcal E(x,0)=x$, $d_v\mathcal E(x,0)=I$, and $\mathcal E(x,v)\in L_j$ whenever $x\in L_j$, $v\in T_xL_j$. The map $(x,v)\mapsto(x,\mathcal E(x,v))$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open neighborhood of the diagonal in $X\times X$ after shrinking its domain. Its inverse for sufficiently close pairs in $L_j\times L_j$ takes values in $TL_j$.

On smaller fixed generator neighborhoods it is exactly coordinate addition:
$$q(\mathcal E(x,v))=q(x)+dq_xv$$
for all sufficiently small $v$. Derivatives of every fixed order of this addition and its inverse are uniformly bounded on smaller neighborhoods in finite coordinate covers. This is a genuine finite-dimensional boundary-preserving local addition, not an assumption about a Sobolev map space.

derivations.claim: Retain a finite number of these charts on the compact parameter-surface space. On an already fixed spatial region retain the given $b$-dependent, $s$-independent charts there instead: their fiber complex-linear derivatives show that their overlaps with every newly constructed chart are holomorphic, and both charts are jointly smooth. When a prescribed point is present subtract its smooth coordinate value, so its coordinate is zero. To form relative symmetric-product charts, take disjoint support disks and the elementary coefficients of their root polynomials. The proof of [F2] that this is a homeomorphism uses only the finite root bound and convergent subsequences in a compact finite product; it is independent of the number of base parameters. Its transition formula is $$p_l(a,c)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{\partial D}g_a(z)^l\frac{P_c'(z)}{P_c(z)}\,dz.$$ The denominator is uniformly separated from zero on each small coefficient neighborhood and contour. Every mixed $a,c$ derivative may therefore be taken under this fixed finite contour integral. Newton identities recover the new coefficients, and the same contour extraction handles changes of support-cluster decomposition. Thus the transitions and inverses are smooth in all base variables and holomorphic vertically, including at every higher collision. The projection is locally $(a,c)\mapsto a$ and is a proper submersion, since its underlying space is the compact finite quotient. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Construct transport in the specified $s$ direction, keeping $b$ fixed. In each relative coefficient chart use the vector with $ds=1$, $db=0$ and all coefficients constant. It is tangent to every multiplicity stratum. Centering a support coordinate at each protected point makes the corresponding incidence condition the zero constant coefficient, so the field is tangent to every protected divisor. Near the fixed off-diagonal compact subset, instead prescribe the raw constant-point field. It is well-defined smoothly there because the roots have distinct labels in disjoint small disks. On a fixed spatial region with $s$-independent charts the coefficient-constant field is also the raw field, even when roots repeat. On a parameter-end collar where the surface structure is entirely independent of $s$, use the raw field everywhere on that collar in its $s$-independent relative atlas. Choose nested smaller prescription neighborhoods, explicit chart bumps and a finite subordinate partition on the compact total space, as in [F2]. Combine the local fields with weights summing to one, taking weight one for prescribed fields on the smaller neighborhoods. Their differences are vertical, and every nonzero term is tangent to the specified stratum/divisor there, so the resulting smooth field $V$ has all the asserted tangencies and prescriptions. No arbitrary-index partition is used. [F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Lift this actual field before integrating it. On an ordered support chart, the coefficient-constant lift holds each individual $z_{a,
u}(x_i)$ constant while $b$ is fixed and $s$ increases. Its root velocity is $-(d_xz_{a,
u})^{-1}\partial_sz_{a,
u}$, smooth jointly in $(a,x_i)$. Equal roots have equal velocities. The ordered quotient map is smooth, because its coefficient components are elementary symmetric polynomials in the smooth root coordinates. Pull back the same finite partition weights by that map and sum the root fields. This is a genuinely smooth equivariant field, related to $V$ by the quotient differential even at collisions. A root at a protected point has velocity zero, and equal roots have equal velocities; hence every coordinate incidence set and pairwise diagonal is invariant. The raw prescriptions lift to the raw field. These assertions use no inverse derivative of the ramified quotient. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

Integrate both fields with $b$ constant, using [F3]. The base $s$ coordinate increases at speed one. Compactness gives continuation to every $s\in[0,1]$ and the actual differentiated ODE gives smooth joint dependence on $(b,s)$ and all initial data. Reverse-time flow gives the inverse with the same parameter smoothness. Uniqueness identifies the quotient of the ordered flow with the coefficient-space flow, since their fields are related. The invariant hypersurfaces are preserved by restricted-flow uniqueness. For multiplicity types use their actual locally closed smooth root-position parametrizations from [F2]; the set of times in each type is open by two-sided uniqueness. The finitely many disjoint types partition a connected time interval, so only one occurs. Thus the flows have all asserted invariances. Their fixed-order derivatives, and those of the inverse flows, are bounded on the compact parameter-product spaces by continuity. This also proves smoothness up to all faces of the cube, using the local smooth extensions when solving the ODE. [F2, F3, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

A prescribed raw field fixes the underlying tuple there, giving the claimed identity maps on each fixed spatial prescription. On a parameter-end collar where the entire horizontal field is raw, continuing the flow leaves its tuple unchanged as $s$ varies within that collar; the tuple arriving at the terminal collar can already have moved earlier, explaining precisely the constant-in-$s$ conclusion. The construction is jointly smooth in all remaining parameters and does not choose transports independently on different faces. It therefore supplies actual square/cube families of transports, but makes no assertion about filling an unrelated boundary trivialization. All limits and inverses were the specified Neumann/flow constructions in the Countable Choice suppliers. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra] ∎

Assume Countable Choice. Let $B=[0,1]^d$, where $d$ is finite, and let $j_{b,s}$ be a smooth family of orientation-compatible complex structures on a compact oriented surface $\Sigma$, for $(b,s)\in B\times[0,1]$. Smoothness at the boundary means local smooth extendibility. For every $m\ge1$, the relative symmetric products $X_{b,s}=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma,j_{b,s})$ admit a smooth coefficient atlas over $B\times[0,1]$, with smooth vertical complex structure. There are diffeomorphisms
$$\Phi_{b,s}:X_{b,0}\longrightarrow X_{b,s},\qquad \Phi_{b,0}=I,$$
smooth jointly in all variables in that relative atlas, and genuine smooth permutation-equivariant ordered lifts on $\Sigma^m$. Both the maps and their inverses have bounded derivatives of each fixed order on the compact parameter-product spaces. They preserve every multiplicity stratum and every chosen finite point-incidence divisor, and their ordered lifts preserve each pairwise diagonal and each coordinate incidence set.

As in the one-parameter construction, the maps may be the raw identity near any fixed compact off-diagonal subset avoiding the prescribed point divisors, for example the union of two product tori. If the structures are independent of $s$ on a fixed spatial region, given smooth $b$-dependent holomorphic charts there may be retained unchanged in $s$, and the transport may be the raw identity on a smaller such region. Prescribed constant charts may likewise be retained unchanged wherever the whole family is already fixed. All simultaneous prescriptions must agree on their overlaps. If the entire surface family is independent of $s$ on a parameter-end collar, the horizontal field can be the raw constant-point field on that collar, so the transport is constant in $s$ there. This does not assert that its value on the terminal collar is the identity.

These are actual smooth finite-parameter transports, including parameter squares used for homotopies. No extension of an arbitrarily prescribed trivialization on the entire boundary of a parameter cube is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented smooth surface with positive area form $\eta$ and an orientation-compatible complex structure $j$. Use its smooth complex symmetric product $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m\Sigma$, $m\ge1$, and the descended product symplectic form $\omega$ off the diagonal. Let $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m$ be disjoint embedded circles, and likewise $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m$, with every alpha-beta intersection transverse. Let $T_\alpha,T_\beta\subset X$ be their product tori. Fix finitely many points $p$ of $\Sigma$ away from all these circles and the associated divisors $E_p=\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}\Sigma$.

The intersection $K=T_\alpha\cap T_\beta$ is finite and disjoint from the diagonal and all $E_p$. There exist pairwise disjoint neighborhoods $U_x$ of its points, with closures disjoint from those protected sets, and smooth coordinate charts $q_x$ centered at $x$ taking $T_\alpha,T_\beta$ to $\mathbb R^m,i\mathbb R^m$. There is a smooth almost complex structure $J_*$ on $X$ equal to $\operatorname{Sym}^m(j)$ near the diagonal and all $E_p$, taming $\omega$ elsewhere, and exactly $i$ in each $q_x$ chart near $x$.

More generally any smooth family $J_t$ with the first two properties can be modified inside the $U_x$, retaining its values outside them and near all protected sets, to have those exact product-integrable values on smaller neighborhoods for every $t$. The constant path $J_*$ therefore provides a genuine admissible geometric choice with the local hypotheses needed for product-integrable end asymptotics. No regularity or moduli count is asserted for that path.

derivations.claim: On the common raw neighborhood of $L_0\cup L_1$, all pulled-back product forms are the SAME form $\Omega$: the underlying tuple coordinates and their differentials are unchanged, and the surface form $\eta$ is fixed. Each torus is Lagrangian there. Indeed locally it is a product of one-dimensional curves in distinct surface factors, so the product two-form restricts to zero, and its dimension is half the ambient real dimension. Its finite quotient changes neither assertion in the actual off-diagonal charts. The standard $K_{b,s}$ is compatible with $\Omega_{b,s}$ everywhere off the diagonal: on the ordered product each surface structure preserves its positive two-form, and $\eta(v,j_{b,s}v)>0$; direct sums and pullback preserve these identities. On the common neighborhood, fix one reference value $K_*$ of this smooth family. It is compatible with the fixed $\Omega$ there. This reference is a fixed endomorphism field, not an arbitrary choice at infinitely many points. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

Record precisely the compatible part of the tame Cayley calculation. For a compatible $K$ put $g(v,w)=\Omega(v,Kw)$. If $J$ is tame, [F2] gives $A=-KJ$, $B=(A-I)(A+I)^{-1}$, $BK=-KB$, $\|B\|_g<1$, and $J=K(I+B)(I-B)^{-1}$. Conversely every such $B$ gives a tame complex structure, since for $v=(I-B)w$ one has $\Omega(v,Jv)=\|w\|_g^2-\|Bw\|_g^2$. It is compatible exactly when $B$ is $g$-selfadjoint. To verify the last equivalence, $g(v,Aw)=\Omega(v,Jw)$ is symmetric exactly when $A$ is selfadjoint. Symmetry of $\Omega(\cdot,J\cdot)$ for a complex structure implies $\Omega(Jv,Jw)=\Omega(v,w)$ by replacing the second argument with $Jw$, and conversely compatibility implies this symmetry. Finally $A=(I+B)(I-B)^{-1}$ is selfadjoint exactly when $B=(A-I)(A+I)^{-1}$ is selfadjoint: rational functions of a selfadjoint finite-dimensional operator with invertible real denominators are selfadjoint. Thus compatible Cayley coefficients form the convex set of selfadjoint $K$-anticommuting operators of norm less than one. This is an actual pointwise matrix argument, valid smoothly over the parameter and spatial variables. [F2, construct, algebra]

Use the finite disjoint generator charts from [F2]. In each, the constant $i$ structure is compatible with the local product form: that form is a sum of positive functions times $dx_a\wedge dy_a$. Compute the Cayley coefficient of this $i$ relative to $K_*$ on that chart. It is selfadjoint by step1.2. Multiply it by a smooth cutoff supported in the chart and equal to one on a smaller generator neighborhood; outside the charts use coefficient zero. The supports are disjoint, and all coefficients have norm less than one. The resulting structure $J_\partial$ on the common raw neighborhood is compatible with $\Omega$, agrees with $i$ in the smaller generator charts and equals $K_*$ elsewhere. This choice is independent of all parameters. Compatibility and the Lagrangian calculation in step1.1 make both tori totally real: if $v,J_\partial v$ were both tangent to one torus with $v\ne0$, their pairing would be zero by the Lagrangian condition and positive by compatibility, a contradiction. Since the union of tori is compact and disjoint from $\Delta\cup E$, choose nested common neighborhoods $N_0\Subset N_1\Subset N_2$ in that raw neighborhood, with all generator subcharts in $N_0$, and a smooth cutoff $\chi$ equal to one on $N_0$ and supported in $N_1$. The structure $J_\partial$ is needed only on $N_2$. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

For each parameter and each point of $N_2$, compute the coefficient $B_{\partial,b,s}$ of $J_\partial$ relative to $K_{b,s}$ using step1.2. Both structures are compatible with the same $\Omega$ there. Hence $B_{\partial,b,s}$ is selfadjoint in the metric of $K_{b,s}$, anticommutes with $K_{b,s}$, and has norm less than one. Define $B_{b,s}=\chi B_{\partial,b,s}$ on $N_2$ and zero outside the support of $\chi$. This extension is smooth. The Cayley formula gives $J_{b,s}$ off the protected set, and set $J_{b,s}=K_{b,s}$ where $B_{b,s}=0$, including a whole neighborhood of $\Delta\cup E$. These definitions agree on open overlaps, so yield a genuine smooth structure on all of $X$, without extending a singular product form across $\Delta$. On $N_0$ it is exactly $J_\partial$, and elsewhere off $\Delta$ it is compatible, hence tame, for $\Omega_{b,s}$. The finite covering and compact parameter set give all fixed-order derivative bounds on compact subsets of the form's domain and on the entire smooth complex-structure family. Common exact generator charts are those of step2.1. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

For the relative endpoint assertion compute the tame Cayley coefficients $B_{b,e}$ of $\Theta_{b,e}$ relative to $K_{b,e}$, on $X\setminus\Delta$, and extend them by zero across the common protected neighborhood where the structures agree. They are smooth on all of $X$. On each fixed endpoint collar regard them as constant in $s$; there $K_{b,s}$ and $\Omega_{b,s}$ are constant too, so they still anticommute with $K_{b,s}$ and have norm less than one. Choose scalar cutoffs $\beta_0,\beta_1$ supported in the disjoint endpoint collars, equal to one on smaller collars, with $0\le\beta_0+\beta_1\le1$. Replace the coefficient in step3.1 by $$B_{b,s}=\beta_0(s)B_{b,0}+\beta_1(s)B_{b,1}+(1-\beta_0(s)-\beta_1(s))\chi B_{\partial,b,s}.$$ Each endpoint summand is defined only on its collar and extended by zero where its cutoff vanishes; choose cutoffs with support compactly inside those collars, so these extensions are smooth. At every point the nonzero terms anticommute with the SAME $K_{b,s}$ and have norm strictly less than one in its SAME metric. Their convex combination has norm less than one by the triangle inequality, so the tame formula is valid. On a smaller common boundary neighborhood, the endpoint structures are already $J_\partial$ and $\chi=1$, so all three active coefficients coincide there; the family still has full boundary value $J_\partial$. Near the protected set all coefficients vanish. On the smaller endpoint collars the formula is exactly the prescribed endpoint structure. No compatibility of the prescribed endpoints beyond tameness is used. [F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

The construction is smooth in every extra cube parameter: all denominators are invertible finite matrices, all cutoffs are fixed smooth functions, and all coefficient fields are the actual smooth families furnished by [F1]. On a compact parameter cube the norms stay uniformly below one on every relevant compact support, so all inverse-matrix derivatives have uniform bounds of each fixed order. This proves both the full two-torus boundary assertion and its precise relative form. Arbitrary endpoint boundary values would not coincide with $B_{\partial,b,s}$ on that common boundary neighborhood, so the proof supplies no such stronger comparison. Analytic positivity or energy for the resulting source-dependent strip equation remains a separate obligation. [step 1.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra] ∎

Assume countable choice and write $D=\partial_s+i\partial_t=2\partial_{\bar z}$ on a connected open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb C$. Let $B\in L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb R}(\mathbb C^m))$, and let $v\in W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb C^m)$, for some $p>2$, solve $Dv+Bv=0$ weakly. Use its continuous representative. Near every point $z_0$ there are a continuous invertible complex matrix $P$, belonging locally to $W^{1,q}$ for every finite $q>2$, and a holomorphic vector function $h$ with $v=Ph$. One may normalize $P(z_0)=I$.

Consequently either $v$ is identically zero, or all its zeros are isolated and have finite order: at a zero $z_0$ there are an integer $k\ge1$ and constants $c,C,r>0$ with
$$c|z-z_0|^k\le|v(z)|\le C|z-z_0|^k\qquad(0<|z-z_0|<r).$$
In particular vanishing on an open set, or vanishing to infinite order at one point, forces global vanishing. The same conclusions hold for $v_s+J(s,t)v_t+Av=0$ when $J$ is a smooth family of real complex structures and $A$ is locally bounded; the local factor is then an invertible real matrix rather than necessarily a complex matrix.

If two smooth maps solve the same equation $u_s+J(s,t,u)u_t=0$ for a smooth almost complex family on a smooth target and have matching infinite jets at one interior point, they agree everywhere on their connected common source. Agreement on an open set suffices. This assertion concerns parametrized maps and actual linear equations; it does not infer moduli transversality or an injective-point theorem.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $m\ge1$ and $2<p<\infty$. There are constants $\eta_{m,p}>0$ and $C_{m,p}<\infty$ with the following property. Let $w\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C^m)$ have compact support, let $A$ be a bounded measurable real linear endomorphism-valued coefficient with $\|A\|_\infty\le\eta_{m,p}$, and let $f\in L^2\cap L^p$. If
$$D_0w:=w_s+iw_t=Aw_t+f$$
weakly, then $w\in W^{1,p}$ and $\|\nabla w\|_p\le C_{m,p}\|f\|_p$.

The same assertion holds on the upper half-plane if $w$ has compact support in its closure and is continuous there with real boundary values. The coefficient need not be differentiable. In particular, localizing a continuous $W^{1,2}$ map satisfying this equation on a disk or real-boundary half-disk gives local $W^{1,p}$ regularity whenever its localized forcing belongs to $L^2\cap L^p$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $p>2$, $\alpha=1-2/p$, and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space. Every $f\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^2;V)$ has a unique continuous representative, and
$$|f(x)-f(y)|\le C_{p,V}|x-y|^\alpha\|\nabla f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^2)}.$$
The same holds on the closed upper half-plane, with its gradient norm and a possibly larger constant. On a disk $B_{2r}$, or upper half-disk $B_{2r}^+$ including its straight boundary, a $W^{1,p}$ map has a continuous representative on the smaller closed disk or half-disk and satisfies
$$\|f\|_{L^\infty(B_r^{(+)})}+r^\alpha[f]_{C^{0,\alpha}(\overline{B_r^{(+)}})}\le C_{p,V}\bigl(r^{-2/p}\|f\|_{L^p(B_{2r}^{(+)})}+r^{1-2/p}\|\nabla f\|_{L^p(B_{2r}^{(+)})}\bigr).$$
The same local conclusion applied to the weak first derivatives implies that a $W^{2,p}$ map has a $C^{1,\alpha}$ representative locally, including the straight boundary.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $G$ be a disk or an upper half-disk in $\mathbb R^2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^{2m}$ be open, and let $J(s,t,x)$ be smooth, including the straight source boundary in the half-disk case, with $J^2=-I$. Let $u:G\to\Omega$ be continuous, belong locally to $W^{1,2}$, and satisfy
$$u_s+J(s,t,u)u_t=0$$
weakly. In the half-disk case assume continuity and local $W^{1,2}$ also up to the straight boundary, $u(s,0)\in\mathbb R^m\subset\mathbb C^m=\mathbb R^{2m}$, and $\mathbb R^m\cap J(s,0,u(s,0))\mathbb R^m=\{0\}$. Then $u$ is smooth locally, including all one-sided derivatives at the straight boundary. Thus a continuous $W^{1,2}$ weak solution in smooth target charts with a flattened totally real boundary has classical smooth regularity. Continuity at a missing puncture is a premise, not a conclusion.

Let $F:M^n\to N^n$ be a proper smooth map between nonempty connected oriented smooth manifolds without boundary. If $y\in N$ is a regular value, then its fibre is finite and
$$\deg(F)=\sum_{p\in F^{-1}(y)}\operatorname{sgn}(dF_p)\in\mathbb Z.$$
An empty fibre gives the empty sum zero. In dimension zero the signs compare the supplied determinant-line rays. The formula is choice-free and presupposes only a given regular value, not a theorem asserting their existence.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map between smooth manifolds. Then the critical value
set of $F$ is a null subset of $N$.

Let $M^n$ be an oriented smooth manifold without boundary. For each compact set $K\subseteq M$ there are finitely many nonnegative smooth functions $\chi_i$ with compact supports contained in connected coordinate domains $U_i$, such that $\sum_i\chi_i=1$ on a neighbourhood of $K$. For $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$ define
$$\mathcal I_M(\omega)=\sum_i I_{\phi_i}(\chi_i\omega)\quad(K=\operatorname{supp}\omega),$$
using the signed chart integrals. This value is independent of the finite functions and charts. It defines a linear functional, is local under restriction to an open set containing the support, and for $n\ge1$ satisfies
$$\mathcal I_M(d\eta)=0\qquad(\eta\in\Omega_c^{n-1}(M)).$$
For $n=0$ it is the finite signed sum $\sum_{p\in\operatorname{supp}\omega}\varepsilon(p)\omega(p)$. All assertions are choice-free: no partition on the entire manifold is required.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed connected Riemann surface, $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ with its standard complex structure, and $m\ge1$. For $a\in\Sigma$ put $E_a=\{a\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$. This is a smooth complex hypersurface, including at repeated tuples. The universal incidence hypersurface $\mathcal E=\{(a,D):D\in E_a\}\subset\Sigma\times X$ carries a smooth complex divisor line bundle with its canonical section, whose zero set is $\mathcal E$ with multiplicity one.

For a smooth map $v:S\to X$, where $S$ is an oriented sphere or a closed disk, define $n_a(v)$ as the degree of the pullback point-divisor line bundle; for a disk use the canonical section to trivialize it on the boundary, and require $v(\partial S)\cap E_a=\varnothing$. The proof constructs this integer by elementary frame winding. It is defined even when a sphere lies wholly in $E_a$.

For a sphere, $n_a(v)$ is independent of $a$ on all of $\Sigma$. For a disk whose boundary tuples have all entries in a finite union of curves $\Gamma\subset\Sigma$, it is independent of $a$ on each connected component of $\Sigma\setminus\Gamma$. If $v^{-1}(E_a)$ is finite and the map is holomorphic on a neighborhood of every one of these points, then
$$n_a(v)=\sum_{z\in v^{-1}(E_a)}\operatorname{ord}_z(F_a\circ v)\ge0,$$
where $F_a$ is any local holomorphic defining function of the smooth hypersurface $E_a$. Each term is a positive integer. Thus the degree agrees with proper holomorphic intersection multiplicity, while divisor containment is handled by its degree definition and actual point movement rather than an unsupported proper-intersection assumption.

Assume Countable Choice. Give an actual complete singly pointed Heegaard diagram of ANY closed connected oriented smooth three-manifold $Y$, with transverse attaching systems, one-ball compression cuts, basepoint $z$, a reference orientation-compatible Riemann surface structure and a positive area form. Suppose it is GLOBALLY weakly admissible: every nonzero periodic region domain with $n_z=0$ has both signs. Broad smooth tangencies of auxiliary compression-disk witnesses are permitted.

There is a choice of surface complex structure, protected region and marked-divisor neighborhoods, common product-integrable generator charts and a nearly symmetric tame path constant on genuine endpoint time collars, for which EVERY nonconstant finite-energy strip with $n_z=0$ has onto actual fixed-end Cauchy--Riemann operator. There are finitely many actual index-one strip orbits with $n_z=0$, across all endpoints and Whitney classes, and their modulo-two count matrix satisfies $\widehat\partial^2=0$. These actual chosen counts therefore define a finite chain complex over $\mathbb F_2$.

Every complete pointed splitting can first be made globally weakly admissible by the finite basepoint-avoiding curve isotopies in [[thm-complete-pointed-heegaard-diagrams-admit-globally-weak-admissible-isotopies]]. Consequently a chosen-data complex of this kind can be obtained from every supplied complete splitting of general $Y$. This does not identify complexes before and after those isotopies. It neither imposes global admissibility on ALL inputs of the original sector-specific definition nor proves the construction for every merely sector-admissible diagram. Auxiliary-choice and Heegaard-move invariance, Spin-c decomposition, relative or absolute grading, plus/infinity and cobordism maps remain separate. In genus zero the empty generator gives the one-dimensional complex with zero differential; a possibly empty positive-genus generator set is not asserted to have nonzero homology.

Let $Y$ be a closed connected oriented smooth three-manifold. A pointed genus-$g$ Heegaard diagram for $Y$ consists of an embedded splitting $Y=U_\alpha\cup_\Sigma U_\beta$, where $\Sigma=\partial U_\alpha$ is a closed oriented genus-$g$ surface and each $U$ is a handlebody, meaning a regular neighborhood of a finite connected graph; ordered systems $\boldsymbol\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_g)$ and $\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_g)$ of pairwise disjoint smooth simple closed curves bounding specified disjoint proper compression disks in the respective handlebodies, each disk system cutting its handlebody into one ball; and one point $z$ off the curves. Opposite-system curves meet transversely in finitely many points. This is closed-manifold data; it includes neither a knot nor a second marked point.

Write $q:\Sigma^g\to\operatorname{Sym}^g(\Sigma)=\Sigma^g/S_g$ for the permutation quotient. The product tori are the images
$$T_\alpha=q(\alpha_1\times\cdots\times\alpha_g),\qquad T_\beta=q(\beta_1\times\cdots\times\beta_g).$$
The group $S_g$ acts on the ambient product, rather than on a fixed ordered product of distinct attaching circles. A generator is an intersection $x\in T_\alpha\cap T_\beta$; equivalently it selects one intersection point on each curve of each system. There are finitely many generators. For $g=0$ the symmetric product and both empty products are one point, with the empty generator.

A Whitney class $\phi\in\pi_2(x,y)$ is a relative homotopy class of maps of a closed disk with two marked boundary points into the symmetric product, taking its two boundary arcs into $T_\alpha,T_\beta$ and its marked points to $x,y$. Its domain is the integral two-chain of complementary regions; its coefficient at an interior point $p$ is the intersection multiplicity $n_p(\phi)$ with $\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{g-1}(\Sigma)$. In particular $n_z(\phi)$ is the basepoint coefficient. A periodic domain is an integral region two-chain whose boundary is an integral sum of full attaching circles. The domain of a class $\psi\in\pi_2(x,x)$ is periodic. Such a class is normalized when $n_z(\psi)=0$. Write $\mu(\phi)$ for the real Fredholm index of the disk linearization, before quotienting longitudinal translation; well-definedness and its topological index formula are properties to be proved in the analytic and index theory.

For the hat construction, **weak admissibility in a generator sector** means that every normalized periodic class $\psi\in\pi_2(x,x)$ with $\mu(\psi)=0$ and nonzero domain has both positive and negative region coefficients. An admissible diagram for the full hat module satisfies this condition at every generator. This is the index-zero weak condition: it does not require mixed signs for periodic classes with nonzero index. In the standard Spin-c formulation the periodic-index theorem identifies this index with the first-Chern pairing of the generator's Spin-c structure; that identification is a separate theorem, not an assumption of that theorem's own proof. One may additionally choose a **globally weakly admissible** diagram, meaning that every nonzero periodic domain with zero basepoint coefficient has both signs. This stronger auxiliary condition is not imposed on all input diagrams here.

For $g>0$ choose a complex structure $j$ and positive area form on $\Sigma$. Analytic data include a smooth path $J_t$ on the symmetric product, constant on actual neighborhoods of $t=0,1$. On a fixed neighborhood of the diagonal and the point-divisors for a chosen interior point of every complementary region, including $z$, it agrees with the integrable structure $\operatorname{Sym}^g(j)$; away from that neighborhood it is tame for the form descended from the product surface area form. The path is chosen in a sufficiently small nearly symmetric class. Product-integrable normal forms near the finitely many transverse generators may be included among its specified auxiliary choices. Existence of such choices and of the regular perturbations needed below remains a mathematical obligation. A holomorphic strip is an actual smooth finite-Dirichlet-energy map $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to\operatorname{Sym}^g(\Sigma)$ satisfying
$$u_s+J_t(u)u_t=0,\qquad u(s,0)\in T_\alpha,\quad u(s,1)\in T_\beta,$$
with uniform generator limits at both longitudinal ends. The space in class $\phi$ is $\mathcal M_J(\phi)$, and translation in $s$ acts on it. Regular means that its actual linearized operator is surjective at the solutions being counted. Local multiplicity positivity, Fredholmness, the class index and compactness are results to be proved, not choices of which maps to count.

The hat diagram-level module $\widehat{CF}(\mathcal H;\mathbb F_2)$ is free over $\mathbb F_2$ on the generators. For regular data for which the displayed quotient sets are finite and, for each $x$, only finitely many nonempty pairs $(y,\phi)$ occur, its candidate count operator is
$$\widehat\partial x=\sum_y\ \sum_{\substack{\phi\in\pi_2(x,y)\\\mu(\phi)=1,\ n_z(\phi)=0}}\#_2\bigl(\mathcal M_J(\phi)/\mathbb R\bigr)y.$$
Here $\#_2$ is parity of an actual finite zero-dimensional quotient. For $g=0$ the operator is zero on the empty generator. That the required regular finite counts exist, that $\widehat\partial^2=0$, and that its homology is invariant under changing pointed admissible diagrams and auxiliary choices are separate analytic and move theorems. Once these hold, the common homology is denoted $\widehat{HF}(Y;\mathbb F_2)$. No filtered chain-homotopy invariant, integral orientations or absolute grading is asserted by this definition.

Comparisons of embedded diagrams permit orientation-preserving isomorphisms carrying $Y$, its two handlebodies, their oriented surface, the attaching systems and $z$ to the specified counterparts, equivalently compatible collared extensions of the surface map. Curve-factor reordering gives the corresponding product identification. Analytic data are transported by the induced symmetric-product map, including $j$, the area form, protected neighborhoods and $J_t$. The intended count identification is the actual pushforward of generators and disk classes with these transported data; its compatibility with the operator requires proof. An ambient isotopy is not assumed to act as the identity. Comparison of independently chosen perturbations likewise requires the continuation theorem.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Pass to physical tuples $v=\Phi_{a(s)}u$. Their equation is $v_s+J_{s,t}v_t=B_s(v)$, where $B$ is the sum of the actual horizontal velocity of $\Phi_{a(s)}$ and $(\Phi_{a(s)})_*W_s$. By [F1] it has a smooth bounded equivariant ordered lift, with norm bounded by $C(|a'|+\|\widetilde W_s\|_\infty)$ and all prescribed coordinate incidences and diagonals invariant. In any relative support chart use its moving holomorphic coordinates $z_a$. The resulting coefficient equation is $c_s+i c_t=F(s,t,c)$ near the protected loci; the derivative of the coordinate with respect to $a$ is included in $F$, not discarded. Its ordered lift is again smooth and equivariant, with the same bound, since coordinate changes and their inverses have uniform derivatives on smaller compact charts. Every coordinate centered at $q_R$ keeps that point zero, so its corresponding lifted velocity vanishes when that coordinate is zero. [F1, A1, given, construct]

Prove the needed divisibility as a BOUNDED assertion, including higher collisions and arbitrary connection comparisons. Write the ordered velocity components as $V_i$. Swapping two roots gives $V_i(\mathbf z)=V_j(\operatorname{swap}_{ij}\mathbf z)$ by equivariance. The finite-dimensional mean-value inequality therefore gives $|V_i-V_j|\le C|z_i-z_j|$ on each smaller cluster chart. For the cluster discriminant $d=\prod_{i<j}(z_i-z_j)^2$, differentiation off its zero set gives $$\frac{V(d)}d=2\sum_{i<j}\frac{V_i-V_j}{z_i-z_j},$$ a uniformly bounded permutation-invariant function. It descends off the divisor and is defined to be zero on it, yielding a specified bounded measurable coefficient. The identity $V(d)=A d$ holds also at zeros: on the smooth discriminant part the field is tangent, and on its singular part the defining polynomial has zero differential. For an incidence equation $e=\prod_i z_i$, invariance first gives $V_i=0$ on $z_i=0$ where no other root is zero, then everywhere on that hyperplane by continuity. Hence $|V_i|\le C|z_i|$ and $V(e)/e=\sum_iV_i/z_i$ is bounded, with the same zero-set identity. Units from other support clusters add bounded logarithmic terms. Thus along the actual solution each local divisor equation satisfies $d_s+i d_t=A(s,t)d$, with locally bounded measurable coefficient, even when that coefficient has no smooth extension at collisions. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Apply [F2] in its scalar complex case. The local divisor equation is a continuous nonvanishing complex factor times a holomorphic scalar function. Its nonzero zeros are isolated and have positive integer local degree: the nonvanishing factor extends over the small disk and hence has zero boundary winding. Local containment propagates through each divisor neighborhood by this same factorization; a first exit from global containment is impossible, because the value at that point is still on the closed divisor and its protected neighborhood is open. Since both boundary tori and the uniform end generators miss every selected divisor and the discriminant, containment is excluded. Their preimages are consequently discrete. They lie in a bounded source interval by the uniform generator ends, and away from the physical boundary by compactness there and disjointness of the tori from the protected loci. Hence each preimage is finite. This proves nonnegative region multiplicities and the finite collision set without a transversality assumption. [F1, F2, step 2.1, construct]

Off that finite collision set take the cover of all ordered roots, of degree $d=g!$; disconnected components are allowed. A puncture has finite permutation monodromy, and each cycle is filled with a source coordinate $\pi(\zeta)=\zeta^k$. The cover is orientation preserving and holomorphic in its source coordinates. Root continuity supplies continuous bounded extensions: on a sufficiently small support disk all roots in that cluster converge to its single limiting support point. On the punctured cover, in the moving holomorphic target coordinates each root has bounded $\partial_{\bar\zeta}$ derivative prescribed by the actual smooth ordered forcing and the derivative of $\pi$. This distribution identity extends over the filled point: integrate against a test on a punctured disk, and the omitted boundary integral tends to zero by the root bound times its circle length. Subtract the [F2] Cauchy transform of that bounded right side. The remaining bounded distributionally holomorphic function is smooth and removable at the center. Thus the roots belong to every local $W^{1,p}$, $p>2$. Their coupled forced equation has smooth coefficients in all root variables; either repeated differentiation with the same Cauchy bounds, or [F2]'s continuous-weak smooth bootstrap on its graph almost complex structure, gives smoothness of the complete ordered lift. This argument does not assert smooth root extraction for arbitrary smooth polynomial coefficient maps. [F1, F2, step 3.1, construct]

On this cover the lifted vertical structure is smooth and uniformly tame for $\Omega=\sum_i\eta_i$. Near collisions it is the product $j_{a(s)}$; off the protected diagonal neighborhood the quotient is a local finite covering on a compact set, so its inverse differential there has uniform bounds. The lifted equation is $f_s+\widetilde Jf_t=\widetilde B$. Tameness, bounded coefficients and Cauchy–Schwarz give $$c|f_t|^2\le\Omega(f_t,\widetilde Jf_t)=\Omega(f_s,f_t)-\Omega(\widetilde B,f_t),\qquad |df|^2\le C\bigl(\Omega(f_s,f_t)+|\widetilde B|^2\bigr).$$ The first identity fixes the sign convention $\Omega(w,Jw)>0$; absorb its last term by $xy\le\epsilon x^2+C_\epsilon y^2$, and use $f_s=-\widetilde Jf_t+\widetilde B$ for the second bound. Holomorphic source covering and conformal naturality multiply the integral forcing bound by $d$. The roots have finite energy on compact filled cores by step4.1 and on the tails by the local unramified generator charts and the assumed finite energy of $u$. The quotient differential itself is uniformly bounded in the actual compact relative charts, so $E(u)$ is bounded above by $C E(f)$ plus the same forcing integral. No inverse quotient bound at a collision is used. [F1, step 1.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

The physical boundary roots lie on the ORIGINAL attaching circles, since the transports and forcing are raw-identity or zero near both tori. For a region $R$, choose a common regular value of the finitely many smooth root maps away from branch values. Their local product-definer identity counts exactly $d$ lifts of each physical incidence intersection. To identify this with the prescribed region coefficient, move that regular test point to $q_R$ along a finite path inside $R$. The incidence line construction works jointly in the surface-family parameter and the moving point: center each local root coordinate at that point, and its overlap ratios are the smooth nonvanishing unit products described below. Pull back this actual line family by the physical section $v(s,t)$. Its canonical section is nonzero on the boundary throughout the point path, because the path misses both attaching systems. Thus its relative degree is constant by the finite frame-winding argument in [F3], even though the transports need not preserve incidence divisors of UNCHOSEN points. At $q_R$ the chosen divisor is preserved by the transport and this degree is $n_R(u)$. Consequently the signed root-degree sum over $R$ is exactly $d n_R(u)$. The preimages of curve edges contribute zero two-form integral: the pullback vanishes on the rank-deficient set, and at a rank-two point the inverse image of an edge is a local smooth arc, covered by countably many source charts. Hence [F3]'s two-form degree formula over the regions gives $$\int_F\sum_i f_i^*\eta=d\sum_R n_R(u)\operatorname{Area}_\eta(R).$$ This is a signed topological identity, not a holomorphic-area assertion. Degrees agree with those on the fixed reference target, with an actual line-family construction as follows. In centered root coordinates the local incidence definer is the constant polynomial coefficient. On an overlap a root change $h_a$ fixes zero, so $h_a(z)/z$ is a nonvanishing holomorphic unit; the product of these units over the cluster is symmetric and has a smooth coefficient expression by [F1]'s contour transition formula. Noncontaining clusters supply ordinary nonvanishing units. These are actual smooth line transition functions on the relative family, with its canonical section and the physical incidence coorientation. Pull this line family back by the actual transports. Finite local projections and their smooth ODE trivialize it along each parameter path, taking the canonical nonzero section as the fixed frame on a common neighborhood of both tori. Such projections are obtained by embedding finitely many local frames with normalized finite chart weights into a trivial finite-rank bundle; projection onto their span is a finite invertible Gram-matrix formula. The same finite differentiated ODE proves the parameter-smooth identification. Relative boundary winding is invariant through this genuine line-family homotopy, by the frame argument in [F3]. Thus its degrees are those on the fixed reference target; raw identity near the tori retains the prescribed boundary frame. Truncate the strip in generator charts and cap by constants; their tail areas tend to zero by the actual finite root energy, and the caps contribute zero. Integrating step5.1 now proves the asserted energy bound, uniformly on the stated compact families. [F1, F3, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

If $n_z=0$ and the diagram is globally weakly admissible, [F4] applies to these same actual domains: their boundary paths are on its fixed two circle systems, and their differences are normalized integral periodic chains. For clarity its real-cone step is essential: a nonzero nonnegative real periodic vector has a nonzero nonnegative rational vector in its rational face, and clearing denominators contradicts global weak admissibility. An unbounded normalized domain sequence, divided by its coefficient norm, would limit to such a vector; integral boundedness is finiteness. Positivity was proved in step3.1 before this use. There are finitely many endpoint pairs, so one finite domain set bounds all area sums without any index restriction. A uniform bound on the actual forcing integral then gives one energy bound by step6.1. For genus zero the target is a point, its operator and energies are zero and the claims are the literal empty sums. No moduli or invariance assertion has been used or deduced. [F3, F4, A1, step 3.1, step 6.1, construct, algebra] ∎
